title: The Alibi of Little Hawley
premise: When the coffin of Little Hawley's founder, Edmund Voss, is exhumed for a cemetery relocation and found empty, concierge Oscar Hartwell is pulled into a mystery that unravels the town's founding myth. Oscar, who has spent decades observing guests at the Hotel Meridian without being seen, discovers that Voss faked his death in 1962 to escape a crime he committed against his business partner—and that a witness, long declared dead, may still be alive. As Oscar closes in on the truth, he realizes the town's most powerful families will kill to keep the alibi intact, forcing him to choose between the invisibility that has protected him and the loyalty owed to someone who once saved him. In the end, Oscar finds the witness—Voss's partner's daughter, living quietly as the hotel's night cleaner—and exposes the truth at the town's centennial gala, trading his anonymity for belonging.
about_author: Y. M. Crane is the pen name of a former small-town newspaper archivist who spent years cataloguing obituaries and land deeds before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about overlooked people who see too much, drawing on a lifelong fascination with the secrets towns tell themselves.

chapters.title: The Man Who Watched the Lobby
chapters.summary: Oscar Hartwell introduces himself through his rituals: memorizing guests' habits, reading luggage, staying unseen. POV: Oscar. The emotional beat is quiet pride in invisibility, undercut by loneliness—he knows everyone in Little Hawley and belongs to no one.

chapters.title: Dirt Where a Body Should Be
chapters.summary: The cemetery relocation crew opens Edmund Voss's coffin before the centennial and finds it empty. The mayor begs Oscar—informally—to keep it quiet while they investigate. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: shock giving way to a thrill he hasn't felt in years; a case worth closing.

chapters.title: Sixty-Two Years of Flowers
chapters.summary: Oscar researches the annual memorial: every June 14th, fresh lilies appear on Voss's grave, though no family claims them. He interviews the florist, who remembers an old woman with a limp. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: first crack in the official story—the dead are being mourned by someone living.

chapters.title: The Founder's Perfect Alibi
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter via the town archive: Voss's celebrated deathbed letter, the statue, the scholarship. Oscar notices the letter's handwriting doesn't match earlier documents. POV: Oscar with archival excerpts. Emotional beat: unease—the town's identity rests on a forgery.

chapters.title: Guests Who Never Check Out
chapters.summary: Oscar cross-references hotel ledgers from 1962 and finds a room booked under the name of Voss's business partner, Daniel Reyes, the week Reyes supposedly drowned. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: cold dread as he realizes the drowning and the empty coffin are connected.

chapters.title: A Warning on the Pillow
chapters.summary: Someone leaves a note in Oscar's staff quarters: 'Some coffins stay shut for a reason.' His car tires are slashed. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: fear arriving late but fully—invisibility was protection, and he's been noticed.

chapters.title: The Mayor's Hospitality
chapters.summary: Mayor Colleen Voss-Drayton, the founder's great-granddaughter, offers Oscar a generous 'consulting fee' and hints the case should close quickly—with the coffin robbed by drifters. POV: alternating Oscar and Colleen. Emotional beat: corruption wearing a friendly face; Oscar smells a bought verdict.

chapters.title: The Night Cleaner
chapters.summary: Oscar notices the hotel's night cleaner, Ruth Alvarez, flinches at Voss's portrait and hums a song from the 1960s. She has worked at the Meridian for forty years under different names. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: recognition—he finally sees someone the way no one sees him.

chapters.title: What Ruth Saw in June
chapters.summary: Ruth, cornered gently, admits she was a child in 1962 and saw Voss alive after his 'death,' fleeing with a suitcase—but her testimony was buried when her father, the groundskeeper, died mysteriously. POV: Ruth (first time). Emotional beat: grief and terror; she has carried this alone for sixty years.

chapters.title: The Witness Everyone Swears Is Dead
chapters.summary: Oscar realizes Ruth isn't just a witness—she's Daniel Reyes's daughter, smuggled out and hidden in plain sight at the hotel her father owned. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: vertigo; the answer has been mopping the lobby floor all along.

chapters.title: Ledgers and Lies
chapters.summary: Oscar reconstructs the 1962 scheme: Voss embezzled the partnership blind, drowned Reyes, staged his own death, and paid off the coroner. The forged letter sealed the myth. POV: Oscar with document inserts. Emotional beat: righteous anger hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: An Offer of Silence
chapters.summary: Colleen confronts Oscar with evidence of his own buried past—a youthful mistake from another town—and offers him money and erasure if he drops it. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: temptation and shame; power knows exactly how to buy a man like him.

chapters.title: The Lilies Arrive Early
chapters.summary: Fresh lilies appear on the empty grave days ahead of schedule—a signal between Ruth and someone else. Oscar stakes out the cemetery and glimpses an elderly man with a cane. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: hope sharpened into urgency; someone else is still paying tribute.

chapters.title: The Coroner's Grandson
chapters.summary: Oscar tracks down the grandson of the 1962 coroner, who kept his grandfather's confession unsent. It names Voss alive in a coastal town as recently as 1998. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: vindication shadowed by dread—the trail is warm, which means others can follow it.

chapters.title: Broken Glass at the Meridian
chapters.summary: Ruth's room is ransacked; her father's hidden letters are gone. She decides to leave town that night. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: despair curdling into defiance—she refuses to run again after sixty years of hiding.

chapters.title: The Man with the Cane
chapters.summary: Oscar follows the lily-bringer: not Voss, but Voss's son, alive and secreted away, who confirms his father lived until 2001 and confessed everything on tape. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: awe tipping into alarm—the tape is the prize everyone will kill for.

chapters.title: Hunted Through the Centennial Preparations
chapters.summary: With the gala two days away, Oscar and Ruth dodge surveillance by Colleen's fixer, moving through service corridors only Oscar knows. POV: alternating Oscar and Ruth. Emotional bond deepens; the invisible man teaches the hidden woman how to move unseen.

chapters.title: The Tape in the Walls
chapters.summary: The son reveals the confession tape was hidden inside the hotel—in the foundation stone of the lobby desk Oscar has stood behind for thirty years. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: revelation as homecoming; his whole life has circled this spot.

chapters.title: Centennial Gala
chapters.summary: At the celebration, Colleen unveils a new Voss monument. Oscar plays the tape over the ballroom speakers: Voss confessing to Reyes's murder and his own fake death. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: climax—terror, then exhilaration, then stillness as the town hears its myth die.

chapters.title: What the Town Does with the Truth
chapters.summary: Fallout: Colleen resigns, the statue comes down, and some townsfolk turn on Oscar for shattering their heritage. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: bittersweet vindication—truth costs something, and everyone pays a share.

chapters.title: The Empty Grave, Filled
chapters.summary: Reyes's remains are recovered and buried beside Ruth's mother; Ruth gives the eulogy under her real name. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: mourning finally allowed; sixty years of silence released.

chapters.title: Concierge, Known
chapters.summary: Oscar returns to the front desk, but now guests greet him by name; Ruth leaves flowers on the desk each June 14th. He takes one last case—a missing cat—and smiles. POV: Oscar. Emotional beat: resolution—belonging chosen over invisibility, and finding it cost exactly what it was worth.
